A Single Handed Route Agent—Negro Murderer Escaped—Boiler Explosion.

GALVESTON, June 20.—A San Antonio special to the News says: The north-bound stage on the San Atonio and Laerdo line was stopped Saturday night near Rice Station, on the line of the International and Great Northern railway, about twenty-four miles from here, by one masked man, who compelled two passengers to alight and assist in rifling the mail of checks and drafts. THE ELEVATOR CO.

At Keokuk Explain Some of the Recent Operations of the Concern.

KEOKUK, IOWA, June 20.—The following regarding the matters of the Keokuk Elevator was printed this evening, signed by W. N. Sturges: "On or about August 1st an agreement was made with Kennett, Hewitt & Co, of Chicago, by which they were to advance on warehouse receipts from the Keokuk Elevator company, charging one cent per bushel on the warehouse receipts, and twelve cents per bushel on grain received and sold by them, upon the following conditions: A custodian to be placed in Keokuk, having charge of all the property advanced on by them, the warehouse receipts to be used by me, and countersigned by the custodian for Kennett, Hewitt & Co. On December 28, 1880, the elevator was closed for repairs, leaving the house and cribs full and 85,000 bushels of oats on the lower floor and one car on the track which could not be unloaded for want of room. This is accepted, with positive proof, that the elevator remained closed from December 23d to January 26th, inclusive. From the closing of the elevator to March 25th I remained in Chicago, with the exception of occasional parts of days in Keokuk. I assigned in trust to L. H. Bisbee, attorney for Francis J. Kennett & Co., my interest in the Keokuk Elevator, pending an agreed joint investigation, to secure them from any contingent, neither admitting nor denying any liability. This investigation, being conducted under the direct supervision of L. H. Bisbee, with Mr. Kennett and myself having

full access to all the books, letters, telegrams and papers belonging to the Keokuk Elevator company, resulted as follows (accompanied by certified statements of all the railroad and steamboat lines running in and out of Keokuk): Amount of corn received from January 1st to June 15th, 196,580 bushels. Amount of corn shipped from January 1st to June 17th, 1,911,451 bushels. Amount of oats received from January 1st to June 17th was 359,656 bushels. Amount of oats shipped from January 1st to June 17th was 359,645 bushels. The property in the house when the elevator was closed was under their charge. Through the r custodian, this investigation has shown by verified statements, in writing, that all employees of the Keokuk Elevator for whom I am responsible, as well as myself, have not shipped the actual receipts from the close of the elevator to date. The difference between the Keokuk Elevator and Francis J. Kennett & Co. are uncertain. The books show an amount shipped for which warehouse receipts have not been returned or account of sales rendered. I have refrained from answering the charges made through the press, awaiting the result. I do not seek to avoid the responsibility of any kind or nature, neither will I assume the responsibility belonging to Kennett, Hewitt & Co. W. N. STURGES."

The Alexander Murder.
Last week, Dockery, now confined in Taylorsville jail made a confession of the part taken by him in the Thompson murder. He says he and Elijah Church, of Wilkes, made up the plan to rob old man Thompson, between them and that Church went there a day or two beforehand and stayed all night in order to learn the habits of the house. When they went to commit the robbery Miss Thompson confronted them but they made her keep quiet by threatening to shoot her. Having secured their booty, they left, but upon reflecting that Miss Thompson knew Church and his name they returned to cover up their tracks." Miss Thompson met them with a gun in her hands. Church grasped her arms, wrenched the gun from her and let her to the wood pile. There, Dockery held her, while Church knocked her in the head with an axe and accomplished the brutal murder. They went to the house of Jno. Adams, on the Brushy Mountains in Wilkes, and gave him one fourth of the booty, and got their supper. They hid their bloody clothes close by Adams' house, which were found by the Sheriff of Wilkes. Adams was arrested and carried to Taylorsville, but was released on giving $500 bail, it is thought in order to prevent having premature developments, which would scare off other suspected parties.

The clue that led to Dockery's arrest was a letter from a postmaster in Alleghany, written to the postmaster at Taylorsville, asking if a murder had been committed in Alexander, as two men, giving their names as Dockery and Church were in his community—acting suspiciously, and spending money too freely for persons in their condition.

IN MEMORIAM.
Death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer—Meeting of the Official Board of Tryon Street Church, Charlotte.

The recent death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer, late of Edenton Street Church, Raleigh, former pastor of Tryon Street Charlotte, has affected the hearts of his former charge with deepest sorrow, and is felt in the whole community. During his pastoral charge of Tryon Street Church, through a period of four years, his ministry was marked by gentleness, faithfulness and ability—the most perfect esteem, affection, and confidence of his flock was maintained, while not a single discord occurred to mar the harmony of the relation between pastor and people.

The impress that he left upon this community was only for good. The fervency of his piety, the purity of, and transparency of his character, the simplicity and geniality of his social life, and the attractiveness of his preaching made him a general favorite in his own Church and won the admiration and esteem of the community.

Richly endowed with these qualities, he was prepared to be a "workman that need not be ashamed"—a faithful shepherd to those "over whom the Holy Ghost made him overseer"—a "wise master-builder" in the temple of the Lord—attractive and loving in the social circle, patient toward the erring, kind and tender in the sick room and house of mourning.

Deeply impressed with his character, we are deeply affected by his early death. We feel that we and the whole Church have suffered a great loss. We feel that the grief of his family is our grief, and the grief of the Church.

Hence, as we are bowed with a common sorrow, we mingle our tears with theirs. While wife, and father, and mother, and child, sit solitary in the shadow of this great grief, our hearts not only feel a kindred pang, but respond in sympathy and condolence to the appeal that comes from bleeding hearts.

Again we are impressed with the inscrutable mystery of Providence in removing a life so full of promise to the Church, just as it was approximating its prime, while there are so many waste places uncultivated and harvests ungathered. The workmen fall, still work goes on. The soldier dies at his post, still the battle does not cease; nor are the banners furled. "God buries His workmen, but carries on His work." So is it ever. We reverence this wisdom. We bow to this power. We adore this goodness. We are subdued under a sense of infinity!

While we stand with uncovered head in the presence of the Disposer of events, and bow our hearts in profoundest grief, we recognize in it the special providence of God, who is "too wise to err and too good to be unkind." Thus endeavoring to submit to the supreme decision of the Head of the Church, and to acquiesce in all the developments of His providence, we, the officers of Tryon Street Church, representing in this case the sentiments of the whole Church, while expressing our own sorrow at the death of our former pastor and friend, desire most heartily and sincerely to express to the bereaved family of the deceased our deepest sympathy; and we do most devoutly pray that God, in whose service he lived, labored, and died, may communicate to them His richest consolations in this trying hour, and so sanctify this afflictive dispensation of His providence as that it shall prove to them a blessing, both for time and eternity.

It was ordered that this communication be sent to the Charlotte papers and Raleigh Christian Advocate for publication—also that a copy be sent to Mrs. A. A. Boshamer as a testimony of our sympathy and affectionate regard.

Mt. PLEASANT, Oct. 20.—Last night a very bold robbery was committed by a gang of outlaws at the house of John Galloway, two miles northeast of town.

Galloway is an unmarried man seventy years of age. He was supposed to have money about his house. Nancy Newell, his housekeeper, aged forty-five, was also supposed to have some money.

Last night about eight o'clock, Mr. Galloway had retired and Miss Newell extinguished the light preparatory to going up stairs when a knock was heard at the door. The housekeeper asked the name. Receiving no reply she called Mr. Galloway, who came down stairs and asked who was there. After some hesitation one of the men said his name was Johnston, when Galloway opened the door. Five bold looking men confronted him. They said they had treed a coon and wanted an ax to cut the tree down, to which Galloway replied that he would not give his ax at that time of night. The men took hold of the old gentleman. He tried to keep them off, but was soon overpowered. They knocked him down, dragged him out on the porch and beat him so badly that it will probably end in murder. He fought for his life and even got his knife out he says he succeeded in cutting one across the hand and another about the mouth. The villains beat him about the head and jumped on his breast to keep him down. A deep hole is cut over his right eye, and in the skull. Both hands are terribly lacerated and one arm badly bruised.

While some of the men were managing Galloway one went into the house, dragged Nancy Newell out on the porch, blindfolded her, choked and smothered her, and offered her whisky, threw her on the floor and actually outraged her. Her feet were tied with a whip lash and her hands were tied behind her with a handkerchief. The villains threatened to blow her brains out if she did not keep quiet.

After the men succeeded in getting Mr. Galloway and Miss Newell under control they proceeded to search the house. They stole in all $2,400 in gold, silver and paper. $1,900 of the money belonged to Mr. Galloway, who kept it in a bureau drawer in a room down stairs; $700 of this money was in gold and the rest in silver and paper money. In a bureau up-stairs they found $500 belonging to Miss Newell. They searched every drawer and even boxes in the garret. Papers and clothing were strewn over the floor. Human blood was smeared over the room and porch, which presented a most pitiful sight to the reporter this morning.

After they had secured their booty they next talked of burning the house, but after some discussion decided not to. About 11 o'clock, leaving their victims bound hand and foot, they quitted the premises. After repeated efforts Miss Newell succeeded in freeing her hands and feet and ran to the house of Mr. King, who is Galloway's tenant. Dr. Fulton was summoned and dressed the old gentleman's wounds. The doctor says Galloway is in a critical condition, but with careful nursing he may recover.

Miss Newell gives the following description of the villains who treated her so basely: The fiend who dragged her to the porch and outraged her is about six feet in height and rather slim, with dark hair and about 25 years old. The one who first attacked Galloway is short and heavy set, is round faced with a sandy musrache, and wore a cap. The other three were young men. She thinks she would recognize all the men again, but don't think she ever saw them before last night.

From the woman's description of the men and from other circumstances there is much cause for a plausible suspicion as to who two of the men are. It has been decided that a Pittsburgh detective be employed. The whole community is be employed. The whole community is greatly excited over the affair. Such bold and daring robbery has seldom had its parallel in this county. It is thought the men were not professional robbers.

INNOCENCE AVENGED.
The Brutal Ravisher of a Little Child Hanged in South Carolina- A Stupid Jury's Work Completed.
CHARLESTON, October 13. — Jack Williams, a negro, who committed a rape upon Linnie Hughes, a little white girl living with her parents a few miles from Orangeburg, in this State, was convicted by a white jury a day or two ago, but recommended to the mercy of the court, which, under the laws of this State, mitigated the sentence from death to imprisonment for life.

The prisoner was accordingly sentenced yesterday to imprisonment. The action of the grand jury excited the utmost indignation in the community, and was very severely censured, particularly as the same jury condemned a negro to be hung for burning a barn. The case was most horrid in its details, and ten of the jury subsequently attempted to clear their skirts of the stigma by signing a statement that they did not know that their recommendation to mercy acted as a palliation of the sentence, but thought it left the matter in the discretion of the court. Public opinion was much aroused, and the general indignation culminated this morning in the lynching of the fiend.

A band of about twenty five men from the scene of the outrage entered the jail about 2 o'clock, overpowered the jailer, took the fiend out to the suburbs of the town, and after obtaining from him a repetition of the confession, which he had formerly made, hanged him to the limb of a tree. Fastened across the breast of the negro was found a placard with the following inscription in large letters:

"Our wives, mothers, sisters and daughters shall be protected, the decision of an Orangeburg jury to the contrary notwithstanding."

The lynching is universally regarded as a righteous act, committed only after the jury had failed in the discharge of its duty. It is a subject of surprise to some that the jurymen were not included in the execution.

Next to the weakness of making excuses is the weakness of accepting them. To be of any use an excuse should remedy the evil which calls for explanation. Reflection will show that a case can hardly be conceived of where any excuse will effect that end. No matter what excuses Grouchy might have been able to give to Napoleon for failing to come to his aid at Waterloo, the excuse could not reverse the historic defeat. The fact was, he was not there at the crucial moment and the result was the same as if he was absent without excuse. Nature's government is the perfection of government; and she excuses nothing. The common law maxim, that "ignorance of the law doth not excuse," is enforced by nature as it is enforced nowhere else. We relieve no disaster by apologies. We take poison with the best intentions, and die just as if we intended to commit suicide. Malaria is all around us and it affects us just as if we had gone there on purpose, although we may actually be on an errand of mercy. Though thrust by another's unintentional awkwardness against the heated stove, it burns us as if we had planned it in malice.

The contrast between this natural government and most human government is very marked. At home children are taught by their acceptance to present excuses often forged and false; and they grow up believing that to refuse to accept them is a cruel hardship. At school the same course of false training kept up, and they come to think that a good excuse is as good as a good deed. By and by they go out from home and school; and as a rule society refuses to accept excuses from all who offer them, and yet insists on their being accepted by all to whom they are offered. The parable of the unmerciful servant is thoroughly human. This morning I read a bitter criticism on the governmental management of a reformatory institution by a business man who has the reputation of never keeping a clerk who has to offer excuses for faults and failures. Yet here is a school which cannot expel its pupils which in his judgment could get along without any punishment in its control of the incorrigible. We can only be taught the absolute necessity of diligent foresight by the refusal to accept or offer excuses. Nature controls all of us. When we go into a room to a stove we first touch it lightly to find out whether it is warm or hot before we lean our hand on it. When we go to a new country we inquire what fruits are wholesome before we eat them. So ship-recked sailors watch what berries the birds pick to find out what are healthful and harmless. When we travel in new lands we inquire into their laws to save ourselves from the penalties of the court. By this method the responsibility of knowledge is put upon the subject. In most homes the responsibility of knowledge is laid upon those who are to govern. So parents hold teachers responsible for being sure that the rules of the school are known by their children before they are held guilty for their violation. The result of this vicious method of home training is that those same children have to learn in the bitter school of hard experience that excuses do not count. Half the grumblers and complainers who fill the world with the story of their unappreciated talents can only justify their own estimate of their abilities on the ground that an excuse is as good as a success. Alas for them, however, society looks at their failures and refuses to entrust them with any great office, and they are unwilling to discharge anything but great obligations.

However this old custom of dealing with offenders may have originated, we find it exercised occasionally in every county and in every State of this country. It is the expression of public condemnation of crime, which, from its aggravated character, will not permit the indignation of the people to await the slow and uncertain process of the law in dealing out punishment to the offender. In border States, where crime is common and difficult of detection and where the law is more or less unsettled, it prevails most, but even in well regulated States we find it meted out in some cases. It is not uncommon in the North, and in our State a number of cases of lynching have occurred since the war.

It is however a rare thing for a person to be lynched after he has stood his trial and his life been spared and when such a case occurs it shows the public mind to be fixed upon the death penalty for certain offences, and that in the interest of self-preservation it will not submit even to a verdict of a jury.

At the late term of the court for Orangeburg county Jack Williams, a nogro, was convicted of an outrageous assault on Linnie Hughes, a white girl, eleven years old, and the jury rendering the verdict accompanied it with a recommendation to mercy. This, under the statute, placed it beyond the power of the judge to impose the death penalty, and he was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The proof of guilt was said to have been overwhelming and the verdict not only created dissatisfaction, but a general feeling of uneasiness on the part of the community. This naturally increased and on the morning of the 13th instant, about 2 o'clock A. M., a crowd of 150 persons, all masked, pushed their way into the jail, on the door being opened to admit a prisoner, overpowered the Sheriff, and taking out Jack Williams carried him about a quarter of a mile and hung him to an oak tree. On his body and fastened across his breast was found printed in large letters on a piece of white homespun the following: 'Our wives, mothers, sisters and daughters shall be protected, the decision of an Orangeburg jury to the contrary notwithstanding.' In cases of this character mercy is misplaced and such verdicts, instead of suppressing crime, tend to encourage citizens to take the law into their own hands and seek security outside the law. It is human nature to forgive murder sooner than such crimes, for the one takes life only, while the other makes life a living, lingering death to the woman. No one will say the fate of Jack Williams is more than a just retribution for his crime, but all will regret that his punishment was not inflicted under and by the law.

Instances of execution under Lynch law are becoming shockingly frequent. They are furnished from all sections of the country, north, south, east and west. Last week a negro was taken from the jail at Orangeburg in this State and hanged. He had been tried legally for a monstrous crime, found guilty, and sentenced to the penitentiary for life. The community was dissatisfied with the sentence, and, at two o'clock in the morning, a mob entered the jail, where the criminal awaited for a few hours his removal to the State prison, took him out and put him to death. Of the particular circumstances of this case we have nothing to say. If the reports are to be accepted as correct, the miserable victim deserved to die, and so probably it has been in nearly every case in which popular vengance has found so horrible an expression. But the question in a civilized state is never. "What does a man deserve?" It is always, "What does the law allow him?" And when the law has spoken, any attempt, whether by a single hand, or by a thousand hands united, to resist or to thwart its decision is a crime. This crime, when it takes the form of lynching, however terrible the provocation, however important the end sought to be secured, and however free from personal malice may be the motives of the perpetrators, is nothing less than murder. It may not be murder in the sense in which that term is applied to the act of a man who cuts the throat of his wife, or shoots his neighbor to death with malice aforethought, and those who are guilty of it may not wear the mark of Cain, nor deserve the gallows. But the question is not what they deserve; it is simply what the law allows them, and the law has no other name for their crime but murder, and no other punishment for it but death.

It is a disgrace to our civilization that lynching exists, not to say prevails, among us, and it deepens the disgrace that such a crime everywhere goes unpunished. It is impossible to believe that lynchers could not sometimes be identified and arrested, yet when was one ever made to answer for his crime? Proclamations are sometimes issued on such occasions calling on all good citizens to aid the government in the detection and arrest of the criminals, but this seems to be understood as a mere matter of form, the people of the community immediately interested smile and shrug their shoulders, and the lynchers go scot free.

Though we thus write, we have no desire to see a hundred gallowses set up in Orangeburg or anywhere else to hang the men who have unlawfully put a villain to death. But we think it is high time that something should be done to vindicate the majesty of the law in such cases as those referred to. What is the good of having a criminal law when it can be thrust aside by any score or two of men who choose to arm themselves and ride up to a jail door at midnight? If the law as it exists now is a dead letter, because public sentiment will not suffer the execution of a large body of offenders for such an offence, then the law ought to be changed and given a form in which it would be effective. If lynching were made the subject of special legislation, and the penalty a fine of not less than a thousand dollars and imprisonment in the penitentiary for not less than one year, we might hope to see the law enforced, and its violation a matter of very rare occurrence. A still surer way of checking the growth of this crime would be to arrest as many as possible of any company of lynchers, and from the whole number found guilty select by lot the name of one upon whom the penalty of death should be visited. Such a law, of course, does not accord with the spirit of our civilization, but it might be better for us if it did. At all events, we pray for something to be devised that shall deliver our country from the shame and crime of tolerated Lynch law.

BOGE JACKSON, The Murderer of Reaen Jordan, Explained His Crime Upon the Gallows at Little Rock Yesterday—History of the Man and the Crime—A Fitting Sequel to a Life of Iniquity.
LITTLE ROCK, November 13.—Boge Jackson, the murderer of Reuben Jordan, was executed at Hamburg to-day. Henry Hill was accessory. Both were first sentenced to be executed October 22d, but Jackson was respited until to-day and Hill's sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. Jordan first had trouble with Jackson about a fence built, but the immediate cause of the affray was that Jordan accused Jackson of stealing a bottle of whisky.

THE MAN AND THE DEED.

Boge Jackson, who to-day suffered the extreme penalty of the law, lived for several years past in Ashley county, way down in the southeastern part of Arkansas. He had been there some time before his previous home became known. The execution took place at Hamburg, the county seat, several thousand spectators, white and black, being present. Hamburg is one of the model little towns in Arkansas, and it is seldom that a crime is committed in that vicinity. The people are all law-abiding and in general strongly commend the enforcement of the law—even to a life for a life. Early in the month of February last, Jackson quarreled with a colored neighbor (both colored) named Reuben Jordan, in regard to a division fence. Jackson's fence was on land belonging to Jordan, and after it had been so decided, he still refused to remove it or to permit it to be moved. When Jordan went to him and remonstrated as to the course he was pursuing, Jordan ordered him out of his sight and commanded him never to again mention the fence. The next time the men met Jordan asked him if he still refused to move the fence, and Jackson told him he would not only not move it, but he would have his life and see if he couldn't then be let alone. Jordan, who was one of the most quiet and peaceable colored men in the county, turned on his heel and walked away, not giving the threat a moment's thought. On the night of February 15th poor Jordan was fouled and cowardly assassinated while walking from the village to his home. The bad feeling between the men was well known, and when the body was found on the following day, the crime was speedily traced to Jackson, who had, to all appearance, taken no steps to ward off suspicion. Even his shotgun, with which he committed the deed, was found unloaded and uncleaned; and on the night of the crime it was ascertained that he was not at home, nor at any of his neighbors'. He was arrested and placed in jail—bail refused. The trial came on, but before the term was reached, it was ascertained that Jackson was a native of Mississippi, where he was born and raised. The States officer visited that State, and learned that Jackson had fled from there to escape the officers. He was well known to the officers of that State, who charge him with three murders, the one for which he was hung being the fourth. He was a sharp, cunning rascal, and made the wormout plea of self-defense serve him well. He was convicted of but one crime in Mississippi, man-laughter, for which he served five years in prison. This murder was that of a poor white man, whose friends did not have means with which to employ counsel. This passing away at the end of a rope causes no regret at his old home. He was a giant in size, a perfect devil when angered, and only thirty-six years of age.

The Horrible Outrage near Reidsville, N. C.
On Friday night last, near the town of Reidsville, Rockingham county, between the hours of 9 and 10 o'clock, two negroes, John Taylor and George Gunn, in the employ of Col. James Irwin, as farm hands, during the absence of their employer and his daughter, went to the house of Col. Irwin and finding Mrs. Irwin alone with her little son, entered the house. From what we are told it was a premeditated affair. The negroes went to Col. Irwin's not to assault or injure Mrs. Irwin, but the young lady who had accompanied her father to Reidsville. Bent on crime, however, Taylor then assaulted Mrs. Irwin. Notwithstanding the resistance made and the cries of the poor, unprotected victim, Taylor accomplished his purpose. Gunn, the other negro, it is said, made no assault upon Mrs. Irwin. He was present, however, and witnessed the hellish act. The negroes then left the premises and went over to Reidsville. Mrs. Irwin immediately went to a neighbor's house.

On Saturday about noon Taylor and Gunn were arrested and taken before a Justice at Reidsville, and during the trial confessed their guilt. The crowd which had assembled, became indignant and at one time lynching was freely talked of. The parties were committed to Jail at Wentworth. No effort was made to lynch them on the way to Jail, but on Saturday evening, it is reported, a number of gentlemen organized a lynching party. It appears that no attempt was made and Taylor and Gunn remained in Jail until Sunday night. During the afternoon of Sunday the Sheriff of Rockingham received information that another party had been organized and that an attempt would be made to take the negroes from the Jail Sunday night and hang them. Anticipating such an event, Sheriff Johnston took charge of John Taylor, the negro who actually committed the horrible deed, and moved off in the direction of Danville, Va. Gunn was left in the Jail at Wentworth. During the night a party of men went to Wentworth, and on reaching the Jail demanded the keys from the Jailor, but were refused. The next thing was to force the Jail doors, which was done, but when it was ascertained that Taylor was gone, the party left and went in pursuit of the fleeing Sheriff and his prisoner. Sheriff Johnston, in order to elude the pursuing party, changed his route and moved in the direction of Kernersville, in Forsythe county. Mr. O. C. Wheeler, the Jailor of Guilford county, met Sheriff Johnston at the depot, took charge of Taylor and conducted him to the county Jail, where he was confined in one of the cells.

Taylor is 22 years of age, weighs about 140 pounds, seems to be in excellent health, and although he is considerably excited, talks freely about the affair. He says, however, that Gunn is the guilty man; that he accompanied him to a point near the residence of Col. Irwin and then stopped. He heard the cries of Mrs. Irwin but was atraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him.
but was afraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him (Taylor.) He acknowledges the fact that he and Gunn were to go together and commit the crime with which they stand charged.

Mrs. Irwin is suffering considerably from the attack upon her. The good people of Reidsville seemed determined to mete out quick justice upon the guilty wretches. Rockingham Superior Court is now in session and it may be that these devils in human form can be tried this week. The people of this entire section sympathize with Col. Irwin and his estimable wife. Mrs. Irwin is said to be about 40 years of age, and is greatly beloved by the citizens of Reidsville and the immediate neighborhood, for her noble qualities.

John Taylor, the African brute, who outraged an aged and honorable white lady, near Reidsville, Rockingham county, has been hanged until dead, and dumped into the soil at the foot of his gallows-tree.

It will be remembered that some ten days ago, Col. James Irwin, a well known citizen of Rockingham, carried his daughter, (a former pupil of the B. F. Seminary in Raleigh,) to attend a concert in Reidsville. Two negroes took the coach horses, and galloped back to the Irwin plantation; apparently unaware that Miss Irwin had come to town with her father. At least it is said they went to the house with hellish designs upon the daughter. The mother, a lady of near 50 years of age, suspecting no ill, sat at home until seized by the two villains. When she recovered consciousness she fled across the fields to the nearest neighbors giving the alarm; then fell fainting, and has been at death's door ever since, if not already dead at this writing.

The two brutes, John Taylor and Geo. Gunn, were soon in jail, and as the country aroused the sturdy farmers flocked in with fixed resolve to give that "short thrift" which is the only real deterrent in punishment. There being some doubt in the case of Gunn, he was allowed the benefit of a regular trial, and now lies in Rockingham jail, free from any danger of lynching. This is right. But there was no possibility of mistake in Taylor's case; therefore he should have gone to the gallows within twenty-four hours after his crime.

Unfortunately the Sheriff being a sworn officer, felt it his duty to save the prisoner for the formalities of the law; consequently took Taylor in his buggy, and fled through by-roads to Greensboro, 40 miles distant. Judge Lynch followed him, thither, but failing to find him, dispersed, until Saturday night last.

RETRIBUTION.

About 11 p. m on Saturday a body of 50 or 60 horsemen entered Greensboro, and being refused the jail keys, cut through three heavy doors, and found Taylor chained to the floor. In half an hour, the cavalcade marched out of town, in military order, carrying the mulatto tied to the back of a buggy. The latter realized his doom; but acted in sullen stolidness, as he has done from the first, refusing to affirm or deny his guilt. To a by-stander in Greensboro he said that all he wanted was to go to Heaven! (Every negro murderer adopts the same tune; and really seems to think he will have nothing to do but step off the gallows into the arms of the angels!)

Seven miles from Reidsville, the lynchers received word that Mrs. Irwin was too ill to permit of any commotion passing the house; therefore the procession halted by the road-side; and Taylor was placed upon the back of the horse he had ridden to do his crime. Being asked if he had anything to say,—he responded sullenly—"Get it over quick!" A sharp switch sent the horse from under him and he fell six feet, breaking his neck. This was about 4 a. m. on Sunday morning.

The news had gone abroad, and from far and near, came the country people, white and black, of all ages, to view the dangling ravisher. Towards evening the coroner appeared, and held inquest. Then the corpse was buried where it lay.

We have no regrets for the lynching,—May we commend it in all except two particulars: viz the delay, and the waving of handkerchiefs by women as the lynchers passed. Judge Lynch should always act calmly, quietly, even solemnly, as if fully conscious that he is usurping the office of the law, but not through passion, sudden feeling, or any other impulse than the grave necessity of Nature's Higher Law,—self-preservation. We repeat that we regret the delay, because the real object of Lynch Court is to set the seal of swift and sure retribution on certain foul crimes! Vengeance should follow within one hour after there is no longer a doubt of guilt. The lynchers should organize a jury and if any three or four intelligent gentlemen will assert doubts as to the prisoner's guilt, let him be remanded to jail to await formal trial. Late in the evening the coroner made his appearance and had the body cut down. A jury was empaneled and at once rendered a verdict that the deceased, John Taylor, had been hanged by unknown parties. THE SHOT GUN.
Further Account of the Riot at Meridian, Mississippi.
The following is from the Associated Press despatches to the Northern papers, and may be true, but it would not be amiss to accept it with several grains of allowance:

MERIDIAN, MISS., Nov. 10.—In regard to the Marion troubles no new developments have been made since Tuesday night, except the arrest of one negro. After the lapse of two days and conversation with 40 or 50 different participants, the recapitulation of the whole affair in brief is as follows:—On Tuesday, while the State election was progressing at Marion, this county, Joseph Barnett, an aged white man, having just voted, was insulted by a negro at the polls. Barnett raised his arm to resent it with a blow. Some say he drew a stick on the negro. Before he could strike, another negro, named Frank Johnson, shot him with a pistol in the neck, cutting the jugular vein and killing him almost instantly. George Johnson, (colored) formerly a slave of Barrett, ran up to defend his old master, and was shot by a negro, from the effects which he died to day, and general shooting among the negroes then commenced. The whites were all unarmed. Jeff Segars (white) was killed by a negro named Sam. Gillespie.

Alexander Harvey, the Democratic candidate for County Assessor, fifty yards from the scene, was rushed upon by negroes and killed by a shot through the head. He was shot in the face by Frank Johnson after he was dead. James Hodges (white) was wounded seriously in the knee. Levy Moore (white) was wounded in the hand. Vince Segars was wounded and expected to die. The negroes doing the shooting were Gillespie, Frank Johnson, Allen and Burwell Brown, and Martin Malone. Marion was not their voting place; they were from another precinct. Will. Vance (white,) Republican, is said to have induced the negroes to begin the firing.

As soon as the news reached Meridian, six miles distant, Sheriff R. L. Henderson, with a posse of 75 men, repaired to the scene. The negroes had all left. A party of 20 men went to the house of Ed. Vance (white,) Republican, and, approaching him with warrants of arrest, demanded his surrender, and were replied to by Vance hollowing to them to go to —. They were then fired on and repulsed, one house being shot. By five o'clock in the afternoon relief came, and the Sheriff, with his men surrounded the house. The Sheriff called out to the people to surrender. A white
Will Vance and his men gathered about the yard anticipating no danger. John Vance was seen in a stooping attitude, behind the corner of the stables with a gun levelled on the horse, but before he could fire he was shot and killed. At the same time while A. G. Warrell, of the posse, was pledging protection to the females of Vance's family he was shot through the head by someone from inside the house and instantly killed. The sheriff and Harain Jones, of the posse, were slightly wounded. Ed. Vance escaped.

Several negroes were seen to fire on the posse from the house and run off. No negroes are known to be killed. Four or five are wounded. Will Vance was brought to Meridian by the sheriff at night, and ledged in jail. No harm was offered him. Young Ed. Vance, a boy of 17 was captured, but was allowed to remain without molestation. Yesterday a party of fifty men went under the direction of the Sheriff, in search of Ed. Vance and others concerned in the riot None were found except a negro named Martin Malone, who took an active part in the riot. He is now in jail.

THE MASSACRE AT MARION. Letter to the Chairman of the Democrattie-Conservative State Committee.
MERIDIAN, MISS., Nov. 8, 1831.
Capt. FRANK JOHNSTON:
Dear Sir:—Condition of affairs in our county is appalling tonight. This has been a dreadful day with our people. Some of our citizens slaughtered—victims of the "six-barrelled code" doctrine. The Democrats are entirely blameless, and (please excuse the expression,) d——d be he who first cries "The Democrats are to blame for it!" The circumstances, in brief, are these:
This morning, as an old white gentleman at Marion was going in to cast his vote he was grossly insulted by one of the most impudent negroes in the county, who had come to Marion from his own voting place, which was another Box. "Lyle's Store." The insult caused the old man to raise his arm as if to repel it with a blow, when a number of negroes immediately fired on him with pistols, killing him instantly. Then A. T. Harvey, Democratic candidate for Assessor, rushed up, unarmed and was shot down and instantly killed; then Harvey's brother-in-law, Joseph Barrett, was killed in the same way; then a man named Jeff Segars—all four good white men instantly killed when they had not a weapon to defend themselves with. Vince Segars and James Hodges, both white men, were seriously wounded, the former with but little hope of recovery. On hearing of it here the Sheriff left on a special train with a posse of about a hundred men, but they found the groes, about a hundred in number, had taken refuge in the dwelling house of Ed. Vance, a notorious Republican, where they together with Vance, and his two sons, William and John, were prepared to make a desperate defense. Our boys were repulsed, and had to come back here for reinforcements. Another crowd from here joined the sheriff, and about 5 o'clock this afternoon the sheriff, with a hundred men or more, arrived there, and was preparing to surround it, when the wife of Vance came to the front gate with a white flag. The sheriff communicated with her, and offered to protect her husband and all in his house, if they would surrender. This being agreed to, some of our boys entered the yard, and were drinking water from the well, anticipating no danger, when one man in the sheriff's party at the well, was shot by some one from the inside of the house, and instantly killed. His name was Mr. Warren, a clerk in Meridian, in the store of Fincher & McMichael. His body will be brought in to-night on the mail train. John Vance, the son of Ed Vance, was killed, and William Vance was captured, and is now lodged in jail. Ed Vance managed to escape by way of the back door, while his wife was offering the flag of truce at the front, and while a number of negroes also escaped, several were shot by the sheriff's posse, as they ran through the bushes. The sheriff himself was hit by a spent bullet in the side, but it is not painful or inconvenient.

Our town is in gloom to-night, especially over the sudden news of Warren's death. Excuse this illegible scribbling. I am writing by a dim light in the back room of a drug store. While on the streets knots of men talk about desperate things that suggest blood. Everything will pass off quietly though. Meridian box at this hour counts out about 5 for Lowry to King's one. Yours truly,

E. H. DIAL.

of the history of the shot gun affair at Meridian, Mississippi, on election day, in which the negroes were accused of raising a riot and of shooting down in cold blood a number of innocent white men. A correspondent of the New York Times evidently a resident of the place where the affair occurred, has been investigating the affair, and after waiting to see the untruthful published report contradicted through some other source, volunteers to do the work himself. The first published version coming through biased shot gun sources, it will be recollected said, that a number of negroes went to the polls armed, insulted a peaceable old white man named Barnett, and then killed him with a pistol shot, the white men around all being unarmed. In the general shooting that followed, two other white men, one of them the Democratic candidate for Assessor, were killed. A white family named Vance, Republicans, were accused as being responsible for the shooting, and the Sheriff with a posse 75 strong, started for Vance's house, six miles distant, to arrest the Vance's and a body of armed negroes, 100 in number, who had barricaded themselves in Vance's house. In the attempt to arrest the Vance family—father and three sons—the Sheriff was wounded, one of the so called "posse" killed, one of the Vance boys was killed, the father escaped, two sons were arrested, one of whom was afterwards released. This is one side, now for the other and no doubt the true one.

Edward Vance and his sons were all at the polls on election day and the usual crowd of negroes and white men were around. Joe Barnett, an elderly white man, was drunk and went around abusing and cursing all negroes who were Republicans. Edward Vance, the father of the Vance boys, because he was a white Republican, was selected for his most bitter curses. Vance, by request of his sons and by Harvey, paid no attention to Barnett, but said he would resent an attempt to assault him. Barnett then went to a crowd of negroes and cursed them and finally went so far as to strike one of them on the head, when another negro said if he would do that again he would hit him with a brick. Upon this, Harvey and a number of white friends with their hands significantly in their pockets, approached the negroes, who knowing what was coming, started and ran.

The white men who lying shot guns reports says were so terribly outraged, pursued the flying negroes fifty or sixty yards shooting at them as they ran. The negroes believing they were all going to be killed, turned and fired with deadly effect upon their pursuers, killing the old man Barnett, Harvey the Democratic candidate, Jeff Segars, also mortally wounded Vincent Segars. The Vances with one white man, a Democrat, and one colored man, believing their lives were in danger, drove home by a roundabout way. About an hour afterwards the house was fired upon, and two of the Vance boys ran out to take a hand in it, but the guns would not go off, the loads having become rusty, and then they escaped back into the house although more than twenty shots were fired at them. The mob then left, but having drummed up more recruits returned with the Sheriff a short time afterwards. Everywhere they went they reported that they had warrants for the arrest of the Vance family, and when they went to the house to serve them they were fired upon by 200 negroes, when in fact the only men in the house were the four Vances, the Democratic friend alluded to and the old negro.

The Sheriff and his crowd gathered at a gin house in the neighborhood, when Mrs. Vance and the Democratic friend went out to see what they wanted, and came back with the word that they had warrants for all in the house The Vances then sent word that if the crowd would disperse and none come to the house but the Sheriff they would surrender. The Sheriff promised protection and started to the house, but the crowd followed. The Vances still kept telling the Sheriff to keep off the crowd but they pressed on, some of them inside the gate. About this time the inmates made an attempt to escape by the back way, but were met by a crowd of armed men and fired upon, one of the Vances being wounded. John Vance exasperated rode upon the crowd and was shot to pieces. The old negro was also killed and one of the crowd was killed. After the firing had ceased the Sheriff came into the house expecting to find all the inmates dead, but all except the negro and John Vance were ready to defend themselves to the last. THE BOTTOM FACTS OF THE MISSISSIPPI MASSACRE. How Colored Men Were Shot Down at the Polls and the Facts Distorted and Sent by Wire to the Country—The Work of Bourbon Devils.
MERIDIAN, Miss., Dec. 10.—After its usually comprehensive style, THE REPUBLICAN has frequently cautioned its readers against receiving as true the reports coming through Democratic sources of the late election riot at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where a number of white Democrats were killed by colored men and Republicans. Marion is only five miles from Meridian, the county seat, where the writer of this resided nearly four years, and, being well acquainted with most of the persons named in the dispatch in connection with the so-called massacre, I have taken great pains to learn the bottom facts in regard to it, and here present them as they come to me through the most reliable and trustworthy sources. My informants, some of them eye-witnesses, embrace every shade of politics; all live near the scene of the riot, and agree as to the main facts.

LAUDERDALE IS HOPELESSLY DEMOCRATIC, but the precinct of Marion Station, when a free vote and a fair count can be had, is largely Republican, and it is the only Republican precinct in the county; hence at every election since the organization of the party in the State there has been "trouble" at Marion. It appears from good Democratic authority that "trouble" was anticipated on the day of the late election. This will be seen from the following: "We encountered a squad of young men of the city last night who are intent upon going to Marion to the election to-day. We think they mean business; and every one of them has a white skin, and, we believe, a white heart. They will keep the peace there themselves to-day, and see to it that everybody else does. They are true, and some on elections."—Mercury (Meridian, Miss.), November 8.

ONE OF THESE "YOUNG MEN"

who went to Marion on that day, being "some on elections," was Moore, the foreman of the Mercury office. Moore has acted as a bully and general fighting man for the Mercury for the past eight or nine years, the editor himself having no capacity whatever for that branch of the profession, though in Mississippi it is the most essential qualification of an editor. It is a melancholy feature in reviewing this matter to learn that Moore escaped with a slight wound. The two Seagers brothers spoken of in the dispatches, one of whom was killed at the polls that day and the other mortally wounded, were young drunken desperadoes, one of them but a few weeks before he was killed having murdered a colored man in cold blood, but escaping the gallows on the ground of "temporary insanity, superinduced by the use of intoxicating liquor." Harvey, candidate for assessor, who also lived at Meridian, was the only one killed at the polls that day whose loss the community will mourn. Joe Barnett, spoken of in the dispatches as an "innocent old man," and the first victim of the slaughter,

WAS THE ONLY DEMOCRAT KILLED

who belonged in Marion or had any legitimate business there other than that foreshadowed by the Mercury. This "innocent old man" (about forty years of age) was the prime mover of the difficulty, as he was first to pay the penalty. When the polls opened, at nine o'clock in the morning, says an eye-witness, there were about forty whites and seventy-five colored men on the ground. Barnett carried a cudgel about two inches in diameter and three feet long, which he used in the most approved Bourbon style. As the situation became more alarming the colored men huddled together some thirty yards distant from the polls, Barnett and Harvey and these young devils from Meridian following them up with sticks and pistols in their hands.
ABOUT THIS TIME BARNETT STEPPED UP to a colored man named Gillespie and demanded his ticket. Upon his refusal to comply with this demand Barnett struck Gillespie with his club, knocking him down. When Gillespie rose from the ground he seized a brickbat. Then Barnett drew his pistol and Gillespie retreated. Some one held Barnett and prevented him from shooting. When Gillespie returned some four or five of his colored friends and relatives gathered round him, apart from the body of colored men assembled. While thus awaiting developments they were confronted by about an equal number of whites, headed by Barnett and the two Seagers, when the fight began in earnest, Seagers firing the first shot

ONE COLORED MAN—ALEX. BROWN—did nearly or quite all the shooting for the colored side. When the smoke of battle had cleared the polls were deserted, and not a colored man was to be found on the ground, but the bloody corpses of the Mercury's "young men" lying here and there told too well the result of the contest. Ed. Vance, an honest, plodding, hard-working Irishman, who lived some three miles from his voting-place at Marion, at once took refuge with his two young boys in his own house. A few negroes living on Vance's place, becoming alarmed, went into the house with Vance for safety, those who did the shooting at Marion having ridden off in another direction. Vance, it may be well to mention in this connection, was a loyal man during the war, and has been a Republican ever since, in consequence of which his persecutions have been enough to drive any man to desperation.

IT WAS DOUBTLESS THOUGHT by the Democrats that a good opportunity now offered for setting the Vances out of the way, as they were becoming quite an important factor in the politics of the county. Accordingly they rallied in large numbers, surrounded Vance's house, and demanded the surrender of all within. The demand was not complied with, Vance being master of the situation, until the sheriff arrived with reinforcements from Meridian, at which time a parley ensued, Mrs. Vance coming out with a white flag and acting as spokeswoman. Warren, of the sheriff's posse, approached Mrs. Vance in an angry and threatening manner, with pistol in hand. Just at this time the eldest of Vance's sons, who had not been engaged in the melee at all, riding up from the outside, was shot dead by the sheriff's posse. Seeing his brother shot down and his mother's life being threatened, one of the young brothers from inside the house shot and killed Warren. Vance, it is supposed, then fled from the rear of the house, followed by the colored men who were barricaded with him, but in doing so a number of the latter were shot and killed.

VANCE IS STILL SECRETED IN THE WOODS, and one of his sons, with some eight or ten negroes, are in the Meridian jail. What their fate will be is hard to tell at this time, but it is generally conceded now that Vance had nothing whatever to do with the trouble at Marion Station. It is important to state in connection with this affair that the Republicans had no ticket in the field in Lauderdale County, and gave only a negative support to what is known there as the "Anti-Monopolists." Consequently there could have been no unusual inducement for Republicans to have precipitated a riot on the day of the election. It is no more than justice to say that Henderson, the sheriff has acted fairly and manfully throughout in this matter, and it is doubtless owing to his influence that scores of lives have been saved since that fatal day.

A girl at Tombstone, Arizona, told her father that she had been insulted by a Mexican boy, in a logging camp, and the friends of the girl went to the camp and compelled the Mexicans to whip the boy until he died. Subsequently the girl said her story was not true and that she had told it for fun.

Russell Schoonover, aged 22, was shot by Daniel Nicholas, aged 15, on the 1st inst. No cause is assigned for the act. Schoonover will die.

An old feud between two families named Ham and Brown, living near Dover, Chickasaw county, Ia., ended in a regular battle on the 31st ult. One of the parties was killed and three others wounded.

Axel Hesman, a young Dane, was shot and killed by Ed. Miller, an ex-policeman, at Chicago on the 1st inst.

James B. Duncan had an altercation with Thomas H. Lowerre, at Chicago, on the 31st ult., growing out of the jealousy of Duncan, who charged Lowerre with being too intimate with Mrs. Duncan. The result of the encounter was that Lowerre, who was a young, stout-built printer, was shot and killed by Duncan, who was an older man in feeble health, and who asserts that the shooting was done in self-defence.

Levi Smith, a young desperado, whose parents live at Leavenworth, Ind., was hanged by a Kentucky mob near Buleyville, Harrison County. He killed a man and fled, but was pursued and hanged by the mob.

A young farmer named John Hopper was found dead in the road near Ramney, about twelve miles north of Lafayette, Ind., on the 31st ult., with two bullet-holes in his body—one right through the heart. It is supposed he was assassinated on his way from the village during the evening, but by whom is as yet unknown. He was a single man.

Francis C. Pease, shot his wife, aged 18, dead at Boston, Mass., on the 30th ult., and then fired several shots into his own body, inflicting mortal wounds. Pease and wife moved to Boston from Rockland, Me., recently.

At Milwaukee, Wis., on the 30th ult., Herman Hilden, aged 17, shot his step-father Bonaventura Krimmer, dead, and dangerously wounded his mother. The youthful murderer surrendered himself to the authorities.

Thomas Duffy had a dispute with Henry Bishop, a clerk in a Fort Bascom, N. M., store, while purchasing goods on the 26th ult., and shot the clerk dead.

Two notorious characters were confronted by officers on a train at Mechanicsville, N. Y., on the 50th ult., when one of them shot Deputy Sheriff Post, of Saratoga county, in the neck. Post returned the fire and perforated the desperado's forehead. The other rough jumped from the train but was shot by a farmer and secured. Besides the wounded above mentioned a deputy sheriff received a ball in the breast, and a passenger carries one in his shoulder. The prisoners gave their names as Lewis Proctor and John Murray.

The body of a man named Neil McKinnon was found floating in the lake at Muskegon, Mich., on the 29th ult. The coroner's jury found that the man had been murdered and robbed. He is unknown there, but is supposed to be a sailor.

At Lick Run, O., on the 29th ult., Dick Williamson and two brothers named Scott and James Tipton quarreled, when Williamson shot Scott Tipton through the stomach and James Tipton through the shoulder. The Tiptons returned the fire, but failed to bring down their game. Scott Tipton will die.

Work of the Flames.

The Delray Glass Works, near Detroit, Mich., were destroyed by fire on the 3d inst. Loss about $50,000.

The extensive rubber works of Eugene Hilapp, East Hanover, Mass., were burned on the 2d inst. Loss, $75,000.

A building at Chicago occupied by Durand Bros. & Co., wholesale grocers, and the Corrugated Elbow Joint Company, was partially burned on the night of the 2d inst. The loss is roughly estimated at $50,000.

The oil country in the vicinity of Bradford, Pa., is being scourged with destructive fires. Forest fires are also raging in the same vicinity, and large gangs of men are out fighting the flames. The damage will be great.

Farmers' Friend Grain Drill factory at Dayton, O., was partially destroyed by fire on the 1st inst. Loss estimated at from $30,000 to $50,000. Insured.

The wine and spirit warehouse, 45 Cheapside, London, the India rubber warehouse of Cowhill & Bro., and seven other buildings were destroyed by fire yn the 1st inst. Loss, $1,000,-000.

Lightning caused the destruction of Otto & Sons planing mill at Williamsport, Pa., on the 31st ult. Loss $30,000.

At Galt and Cheapside, Ont., a welcome rain storm was experienced, but accompanying lightning killed two people and destroyed several barns.

J. G. McElwee & Co.'s picture-backing factory and mills at Big Rapids, Mich., burned on the 31st ult. Loss, $25,000; insurance, $6,000. Forty men are thrown out of employment.

Time has slipped away from me so fast this week that only this morning the fact dawned upon me that Saturday had arrived and my work not half completed, and among other thing my weekly contribution to the Citizen was yet unwritten history.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES
An Oil-Laden English Bark Destroyed by Lightning—One Sailor Drowned and the Captain and Others of the Crew Injured—Four People Killed and Eight Injured by Lightning near Decatur, Ala.—Desperate Fight Between Whites and Blacks in Arkansas—Cattle Fire at Buffalo, N. Y.

STRUCK AND BURNED BY LIGHTNING.

PHILADELPHIA, July 8.—The British bark Beatrice, Captain Stewart, for Rover, with oil, was struck by lightning while off Reedy Island. The fluid ran down the main mast into the hold, and fired the cargo. An explosion followed, and the main hatch was blown into the river, and a sailor with it, who was drowned. Captain Stewart, the mate and two sailors were injured by flying timbers. The vessel burned to the water's edge.

A PLUCKY WIFE.

MANCHESTER, N. H., July 8.—Two burglars, giving the names of Thomas Callahan and Dominick Moran, were discovered at Piscassaquog early this morning in the bedroom of F. Hutchinson, rifling his pockets. Hutchinson seized Callahan and in the struggle both fell down stairs. Mrs. Hutchinson, with a revolver, ran to the aid of her husband, pounding the burglar's head and face severely, and enabled her husband to secure him. He then telephoned the police, who jailed the burglar, and pursued and captured Moran.

RACE CONFLICT IN ARKANSAS.

LITTLE ROCK, July 8.—Intelligence reached here this morning of a serious disturbance at Mineral Springs, Howard county. Wednesday the negroes had a barbecue near town. In the evening they flocked to the Springs in large numbers.
Two who became involved in a quarrel were arrested therefor. At an early hour yesterday the trial began, and the negroes began to congregate, each with a musket or shotgun. By 10 o'clock 200 or more were in town, nearly all of whom were armed. The white citizens, fearing trouble, prepared their guns and placed them in convenient places. At 1 o'clock one negro was arrested for drunkenness and disorderly conduct, when the negroes showed a determination to take him from the officers, and a riot occurred. Almost instantly forty or fifty white men were on the streets with guns. Fortunately no one was hurt. One or two shots were accidentally fired in the air. A number negroes were arrested. Matters are now quiet, but further trouble is apprehended.

HANGED.

NEW ORLEANS, July 8.—Samuel Trivias was hanged this morning in Alexandria, Rapid parish, for the murder of A. J. Hanna.

KILLED BY LIGHTNING.

DECATUR, Ala., July 8.—During a thunderstorm last evening lightning struck a barn where a number of people had sought refuge, and four were killed and eight seriously injured.

CATTLE BURNED.

BUFFALO, July 8.—The large feeding barns of J. Firmenich, near the stock yards, containing about 800 cattle, burned. Three hundred and sixty-two cattle perished. Loss $28,000; insured.

GREENVILLE, October 20.—A few days ago a young man named Waldo Lewis was arresd on a charge of burglary and theft of money from one Mr. Merrick. The case was brought before the examining court, but the trial was postponed until yesterday and the defendant was released on bond. Last night four men, Charley Merrick, B. F. Collier, Mike Lackey and Blank, one of whom represented himself as an officer, went to Lewis' house, took him out six miles to Tidewell thicket and threatened to hang and shoot him if he did not tell where the money was. They proceeded to Morris' house, into which, when reached, Lewis ran, crying murder, and the party fired upon him. Morris demanded their authority for arresting Lewis, and on their failing to show any he ordered them away. Lewis' statement in regard to the money was a ruse in order to save his life. perry-thompson-vicksburg-1881-10-28.A25:
COWARDLY MURDERS.
The Mississippi Plan--What a Liberal Or gan Has To Say About It.
The Vicksburg Herald says of the recent assassination in Sharkey County, Mississippi: "In all our experience we do not remember to have read of such cold-blooded, brutal, causeless murders. Nothing whatever is alleged against the poor, defenseless victims. Perry Thompson, the colored man killed on the spot, is reported to us as one of the first colored citizens of the county. He had the respect and esteem of all, without regard to party. He never did any man a harm, and no living soul had any just cause to harm a hair of his head. We are not informed as to the personnel of the other victims, but we can hardly conceive of anything that will in the least excuse the horrible manner of their death. The assassins fired into a crowd, and seem to have been utterly careless as to the effect. They did not even take the trouble to try and murder particular individuals. Their purpose seems to have been to kill a number of "niggers" and they succeeded. For the horrible crime there is not a particle of justification. Beyond the fact that certain colored people in the county intended to vote for one set of local candidates instead of another there was not the slightest excuse for the horrible deed. The only cause of the assassinations is a scramble for the county offices. There is little or no contention in the county over the State ticket, but there is the greatest bitterness about the local offices. This bitterness culminated in the cowardly murder of three innocent men and the wounding of two others."

pete-megley-1881-05.A1:
Reported Lynching.
News reached here a few days ago that Pete Megley and a man named Wheeler, were found strung up to a tree in Long Valley last Sunday. There has been considerable ill-feeling against Megly and some of his crowd by the cattle men of northern White Pine for a long time past, and we learn that he has been warned to leave the country some weeks ago, and fifteen days given him him to settle his business affairs. He declined to consider the proposition. As we have no particulars of the affair, save the bare assertion that the men were found hanging to a tree as above stated, we do not not vouch for the correctness of the matter; indeed, we are rather inclined to discredit the story.

P. S.—Since the above above was in type we learn it was was only one of Mother Kelly's dreams. The pious Frogtown dame dreams some wonderfully good things, and it's pity they don't turn out true.
pete-megley-1881-05.A2:
Probably Groundless Rumors.
Rumors were flying about town yesterday to the effect that a man had been found swung up to a tree somewhere over in the direction of Hamilton. Some of the stories had it that the alleged remains belonged to Pete Megley, and others that Tom. Glenn owned them. Two weeks ago the Cherry Creek News published an account of the rumored hanging of Megley in Steptoe Valley, but contradicted the story in the same issue, regretting that it was not true. Doubtless this item in the News furnished the basis of the rumors which gained currency in Eureka yesterday. If there has been any hanging done by our White Pine friends it was for the prevalent offense of cattle stealing. The SENTINEL, however, does not believe that anybody has been hung. Hanging is not fashionable in the Great East.

An Alleged Cattle Thief Hanged.

The Eureka Leader of last Wednesday reported a rumor that Peter Megley, a butcher of Hamilton, had been hung in Antelope Valley for cattle stealing. Was Pete Megley Lynched?
For three or four weeks there have been various rumors to the effect that Pete Megley, who made his headquarters at Antelope Springs, had been found hanging in one of the valleys west of here. The rumor, though at first believed, was afterwards contradicted, and a report circulated that he had gone to Wood River. Pete was in bad repute among the cattle men in this county, and was no doubt thought a hard customer to get rid of. From the various reports that have reached us from time to time in regard to the matter, we had come to the conclusion that Pete was still on the mercy side of the river, but yesterday we were informed by a gentleman in this town of facts which lead us to firmly believe he has crossed over to that land where cattle do not roam at large and lynching is not on the bill of orthodox punishment for transgressions committed either in the flesh or spirit. The tragic end of Billy LeRoy, the stage robber, brings to mind a joke perpetrated at his expense by Judge Hallett, of the United States court. On calling up LeRoy for sentence, the judge asked him his age, and the prisoner responded gruffly, "twenty three." The judge then proceeded to sentence the prisoner to ten years to the penitentiary, adding, "That will make your age just thirty-three when you are discharged, young enough to become a member of congress or an Indian agent." Judge Hallet does not often indulge in sarcasm, but when he does it is effective.

William Le Roy's Escape—A Dime Novel in One Chapter.
When Deputy United States Marshal Cantril returned to Denver last Monday afternoon with the tidings that Wm. Le Roy, the dashing road agent and prince of mail robbers, had made his escape while en route to the 'Government Prison at Detroit, under ten years' sentence, the United States officials here were as puzzled as they were angry. That Le Roy should have made his escape from Sim Cantril and a deputy only served to increase their anger and fan it into a flame of no small magnitude. Yesterday the News reporter, in passing the excavation for the sewer at Holladay street, felt a hand clasp on the arm, and turning, saw the mysterious train-wrecker who had manifested so much interest in Le Roy's case, as detailed by General Cameron a couple of days before. "You have not forgotten me, have you?" he questioned in a moderate tone of voice. "Now, as you have manifested some interest in Le Roy's case, I'll give you the whole story."

"When Billy was sentenced I was within easy call, and since that time I have not been asleep. Some years ago the boy used to be with a snide variety company and played the character of a female impersonator, and he was well up in his business, too, and if he had stuck to it would not have been compelled to go to holding up coaches on the road for a living. His old girl, who has been with him from time to time for three years, and who loves him better, if anything, than I do, lives in Del Norte, and we rung her into the scheme with us. As planned by Billy it was to bring her up to town and get two suits of clothes for her just exactly alike—that is dresses of one color, shawls of one color and hats and veils of one color. Then we were to get a suit of clothes, men's clothes, for Billy, and the extra woman's rig and men's clothes were to be kept ready for a close call. We were to keep a close lookout for the time when he was to be taken away, get on the train with him, and then at the first opportunity which offered at night we were to take whatever guards were with him, put up a job on them, and dress Billy like the girl. Then we could go on our way rejoicing.

“The day came and we knew all about it, and when the carriage containing Le Roy and his guards drove up to the train, the girl and I were already on board. They took one double seat and we took the one directly behind them and awaited developments. Along in the night all the passengers got to sleep. We were in a sleeping-car, if it was not called such, and Cantril’s boy got awful sleepy. I felt sorry for the poor fellow, and was glad when he went into the car for a nap. Billy was also very tractable. Cantril was thirsty that night, and I put up a job on him. Going to the water tank, after gauging his drinks and the time between them, I poured out some croton oil and left it in the cup. Then I pretended to take a hearty drink and made so much noise about gulping it down that Cantril got awful thirsty. I had no more than gained my seat till he made a dive for the tank, and without tilting the cup filled it and emptied it. To partially kill the stench of the croton I had put a dash of burned liquor in it. If Cantril tasted anything wrong in the water he attributed it to his sour stomach, and so said nothing. It was not many minutes until the Deputy Marshal felt a general weakness about his bread-basket. When Cantril left and slammed the door to, we acted. All of us were up and doing in a second, for none of us had beer asleep. The irons were off Billy in less than ten seconds, and the extra suit of woman’s toggery was put on him. When all was finished he curled down in my seat, just like the girl had been, and the girl got up and skipped into another car. My next move was to put my head over on Billy’s shoulder, and in another moment the brakeman came in. As he passed by with his lantern I raised up as if awoke by the noise and the light, and; discovering that the prisoner was gone, raised the hue and cry. The brakeman took it up, everybody woke up, and Cantril came out of the toilet-room. Then ensued a scene of confusion. He wanted the train stopped, and the conductor would not stop it until he got to Hays City, five miles away. When we got there the girl got off, Cantril got off, and his assistant with him, and Billy and I went on with the train, tickled almost to death."

"Where is Le Roy at the present time?" asked the reporter.

"He is safe," was the reply.

Judging from the statement made by the train-wrecker, Le Roy has gone East for a time, but will soon return, place himself at the head of his gang and once more take the road.—Denver News.

SUNBEAMS.
Many of the old Whigs in Virginia have joined the ranks of the Readjuster party in that State.

The evidence in a San Francisco divorce suit was all found in a diary which the defendant kept.

Field Marshal von Moltke has very small feet and narrow, long hands; Prince Bismarck has large feet and big, fleshy hands.

There is no doubt about it: people are retrenching on all sides, says the London World. At Christie & Manson's last week a single china plate brought only ninety pounds.

Sarah Bernhardt is again the lioness of Paris. Alexandre Dumas, Jr., went to Havre to see her disembark, and, on shaking hands, exclaimed: "This is a return from the other world!"

The experimental boring for the tunnel between Dover and Calais has been extended under the Channel a distance of three hundred feet. Progress is feasible at the rate of thirty feet a day.

The wife of an old colored man in the eastern part of Georgia recently presented him with the sixth pair of twins, the family having been previously endowed with two pairs of triplets, all flourishing.

King Humbert's course in applying to Sella to form a Cabinet, while the Left was in the majority in Parliament, has been denounced as unconstitutional. The King favors the "Right," just as the anti-Liberal parties are favored by the European monarchs.

Tobacco is prohibited to the students of Oberlin College, Girard College, and the Naval School at Annapolis. A similar rule has been recommended for West Point by the Board of Visitors. At Cornell University nearly all the students have voluntarily signed a pledge of abstinence.

—The new aesthetic craze, says the London World, has been a great blow to the young curates of the period. Instead of embroidering slippers and decorating churches, maiden ladies, elderly and otherwise, now devote their spare time to the pursuit of the "intensely intense" and the "too utterly utter."

—So greatly did Queen Victoria admire the wedding dress of Lady Brooke (the beautiful Miss Maynard, just married to the Earl of Warwick's eldest son), that she insisted on her dining in it at Windsor Castle, and, after dinner, told the bride to walk about, that she might see it better—the result of these peripatetic movements being that her ladyship was "commanded" to be photographed therein.

—Haverly's new theatre in Chicago is to have a peculiar feature, which the owner thus describes: "I have constructed two fashion boxes, which are a novelty, and which I think will take well. These are one on either side of the stage, built level with the floor, and so arranged that the ladies occupying them may be seen entirely. By this means they are enabled to display their toilets. This is the purpose of the fashion boxes."

—Mr. Labouchere, who owns Pope's Villa, on the Thames, where he resides during the summer, writes the following as among the annals of the boating season on that classic river: "A friend of mine, under the influence of a spring evening, moonshine, and other romantic surroundings, was led on to ask a pretty but somewhat strong-minded young lady to 'row in the same boat with him for life.' 'On one condition,' she answered promptly, 'and that is that I steer.'"

—When Gambetta was speechifying at Cahors recently, a cafe-concert songstress was engaged by an energetic manager to sing at the same time to the citizens. This lady, Mme. Gambetta by name, moreover claims to be a cousin of the ex-dictator. His friends, aware that ridicule kills in France, besought her to leave the city, but she replied: "No, I am earning my bread, and will not leave. Besides, what do you take me for? I have been engaged, and when I sign a contract I never break it!"

—The number of works exhibited in the Paris Salon this year shows a notable decrease compared with the Salon of 1880. In that year 7,235 works were exhibited; the number in the present year is 4,932. These are exhibited by 3,668 artists, of whom 649 are women. The proportion of strangers is large—612 out of 3,668. Of the strangers nearly one-fourth are Americans. Of these there are 142. Italy supplies 70 contributors; Great Britain, 62; Belgium, 50; Switzerland, 47; Spain, 41, and Russia, 7. The minor States are also represented.

Garibaldi on the Tunisian question is published by the Rifoma, in which the General says that the French treaty with the Bey effaces his good opinion of the French republic, which he has served. The writer reminds France of the sacrifice made by Italy in giving up Nice, and says that the conduct of France may compel Italians to remind her that Nice and Corsica are as much French as he, Garibaldi, is a Tartar. The letter concludes by declaring that Italy should demand the complete independence of Tunis.
After Capt. Fritz, a San Francisco politician of local prominence, had committed suicide, the police found him hanging with his wrists fortuitously together with handcuffs, while on his ankles were shackles. The keys were produced by his wife, who explained that the irons had nothing to do with the suicide, but had been habitually worn. Politics took him away from home a great deal at night, and in order to compel himself to stay in occasionally he would thus manacle himself, give Mrs. Fritz the keys, and tell her to keep him a prisoner till morning.

On May 24 Queen Victoria attained her 62nd birthday, an age which has been exceeded by eleven only of the sovereigns of England, dating from the Norman conquest—namely, Henry L., who attained 67 years; Henry III., 65 years; Edward L., 67 years; Edward III., 65 years; Queen Elizabeth, 69 years; James II., 68 years; George I., 67 years; George II., 77 years; George III., 82 years; George IV., 68 years, and William IV., 72 years.
