The Grand Duke Nicolai Constantinovich has been transferred from Pavlovsk, where he has been in confinement since his arrest a few weeks ago, to the fortress of Dunaburg, in which stronghold his imperial cousin has decreed that he shall pass the remainder of his days. This unfortunate young gentleman's eccentricities have been the source of much disquietude and distress to his family for some years past. Abundant proofs have been furnished to the Czar that his kinaman has propagated Nihilistic doctrines among the workmen employed in certain manufactories situated upon his own estates, and moreover that, disguised under an assumed name, and in the company of a recently arrested Colonel of gendarmerie, he has upon more than one occasion attended secret meetings of discontented operatives, at which he has pronounced harangues inciting his hearers to open revolt against the State.

—Arthur and Samuel Pond, brothers, went fortune hunting in Colorado. After trying in vain several honest means of making money fast, they decided to become highwaymen, though previous to going West they had been respectable residents of Pennsylvania. They were remarkably daring in their stage robberies, and soon became notorious under the assumed names of Billy Leroy and Louis Potter. They would bob up in front of a coach, fire at it, perhaps wound some of the passengers, give the impression that a supporting band of robbers was concealed close by, empty all the pockets, and skurry away. This exploit was repeated half a dozen times. The enterprising brothers had accumulated a handsome amount of money, when public sentiment precipitated a disaster. The men of Del Norte went out and hunted the Ponds for several days, shot them down, and hanged their riddled bodies to a tree.

Mail Stage Robbers Photographed After Being Hang.

Dr. H. M. Bishop, of this city, the druggist, corner of State and Humphrey streets, has received a letter from his brother, Judge Bishop, of Lake City, Colorado, enclosing a photograph of the two notorious United States mail stage robbers, Billy Leroy and brother, who operated so successfully in that part of the United States and for a long time successfully avoided arrest, strenuous efforts to capture them being long unavailing. At last they were captured, thoroughly identified, confessed and hung at Del Norte. The photograph was taken after they were stiffened with death, one braced up, one against the other, against the jail wall. One was shirtless and his trousers leg was rolled up to show the mark of the bullet wound where the sheriff's gun took effect. The mails had been frequently robbed and the execution of the robbers much relieved the people of these parts. The desperadoes were found in hiding in a swamp, having been hungry for two days and awaiting the return of a confederate sent for food.

A COLORADO LYNCHING.
Details of the Capture and Exploits of "Billy Le Roy, the Bandit."
weeks ago the people of many communities in Colorado were made angry by the escape of the notorious highwayman, Billy Le Roy, from Deputy Marshal Cantril, on the Kansas Pacific express. The story of the escape, as printed at the time, was that Le Roy's sweetheart had planned her lover's release and that she had successfully bewitched the deputy marshal. The true story, as related by the bandit to Dr. Flournoy, of Del Norte, is as follows: Le Roy carried about his person a tiny key, made from a watch spring. When he was stripped and searched on the morning of his departure for Detroit he creased the skin of his neck and placed the key in the crease. His mouth was opened, his hair brushed and his ears examined, but the key escaped the notice of the searchers. When the train was running at terrific speed Cantril left his prisoner, shackled hand and foot, and stepped to the toilet-room. "In two seconds," said the bandit to Dr. Flournoy, "I had my hands free and in another two seconds my feet also. All the passengers in the car, except one lady, were either nodding or half asleep. I knew how to settle the lady. I just gave her one look, ran to the platform and jumped off. I was stunned, but came to in a little while and got away." Several days passed after Le Roy's escape, and the people hoped that he had gone to some other corner of the world. On the night of the 13th ult. the down time for Del Norte passed the lower corner of Franklin's ranch, when from one side of the dark highway there arose a demand to halt. The quick movement of the robbers frightened the coach horses. Old Jimmy—so he is called—was driving, and he had terrible work to control the horses, though he did his best. The robbers, mistaking the runaway for a deliberate attempt on the part of the driver to evade their clutches, fired a volley into the fast-flearning. "Let's go back and surrender," said Jimmy; "if we don't they'll kill me next time."

"For God's sake don't go back," pleaded a passenger, "for I have got $700 on me now and I will lose the whole of it."

So Jimmy put lash to his horses and the coach got away as quickly as possible. Then Jimmy resigned. He did not propose to be killed in any such style. He knew that the bandits were none other than Billy LeRoy and his party.

Le Roy was next heard from when the stage was ascending the hill about three miles from Antelope Springs and about a mile and a half from the lake. The hill is very steep, and it was while the ascent was being made that the agents jumped from their concealment and fired a whole handful of bullets into the passing vehicle. One of the bullets took effect in the leg of Engineer Bartlett, of the Denver and Rio Grande road, striking him in the fleshy part.
The ball struck a silver dollar in Bartlett's pocket and sent the dollar into the flesh, then glanced and went through the leg and out. The silver piece protected the femoral artery and saved Bartlett's life. Bartlett says there were three men in this party, and that one of them—a little fellow—said to the big man of the crowd: "Get on the other side, there, and tend to business." The little fellow pulled his self-acting British bulldog and dumbed up on the wheel. He pointed the muzzle at Bartlett's head and remarked:
"I am going through you; hold up your hands."
The operation required but a short time. Money and watch soon passed into the deft fingers of the road agent. It became necessary to get into the pocket nearest the wound.
"You are hurting my leg very much," mildly protested the victim.
"Well, you can't stand it," was the reply. The front boot was then cleared of mail, and the rear one being empty, the driver was told to go and that "deuced quick." The inside men were not disturbed. The robbers were evidently nervous, for it was early in the evening—8:20. The "little fellow" was Le Roy himself.

The three hunters went toward Alamosa. On the road they saw a little fellow with a pack on his back. At the command "halt" the little man drew a revolver, fired and ran. Armstrong sent a load after him. The ball struck the fellow, and with a quick bound he entered the bush near at hand and rolled down the river bank out of sight. It was a job getting him out of the copse. He would not say a word, and all the coaxing in the world seemed to have no effect. Finally they got to talking about shooting into the copse after him, and this brought the young man to time. He said he was shot and couldn't walk. But they got him out at last, and found that the whole of his calf had been scooped out by the bullet. It was an ugly wound.

"Who are you, anyhow?" he was asked.

"I am Billy Le Roy," he replied.

"Billy the bandit?"

"The same."

Del Norte was crazy over the capture. "The people were wild," said General R. A. Cameron, who happened to be in the place; "the streets were like so many hives of mad bees." The sheriff locked the two prisoners in the rear cells of the strong jail, and a committee of influential citizens were appointed to act as guard for the night. About 10 o'clock the sheriff stepped across the way on business. He was seized, locked in a room and kept under guard. Everything was quiet. Apparently everybody had gone to bed. At 11 o'clock a party rode up to the jail door and knocked. The guard asked what was wanted. "This is your relief; walk out." The guard walked out and were seized and bound, one by one. The party then went directly to the cells where Le Roy and Potter were, took them out, gagged them and left the jail with the prisoners. Not a word was spoken.

At 12 o'clock, midnight, a man rapped at Coroner Holland's house. Holland put his head out at the window.

"Hello!" said he.

"There's two men hanging on a tree near the river."

"What?"

"That's what I said; and, by the way, it's very curious, but I found the keys of the jail just up the street. ere they are."

The stranger tossed the keys in at the window and walked away. The coroner went to the river and cut down the dead bodies, which were those of Leroy and Potter. The next day the coroner's jury found a verdict exonerating all concerned in the affair.

As the dead bodies were stretched side by side many persons remarked upon their close resemblance. Upon Le Roy's right arm were tattooed the letters "A. P," and upon Potter's right arm the letters "S. P." Le Roy's real name was Arthur Pond, and Potter's real name Samuel Pond, and the dead men were brothers.

On Friday evening, July 1st, a party of masked men rode up to Mr. A. B. Hamilton, who was bringing to Benton the man, Brackett E. Stewart, who was charged with the murder of Mrs. Armstrong and O. H. Morgan, leveled their guns at him, and demanded his prisoner. These men were immediately after joined by about twenty more, and they took the prisoner by force from Mr. Hamilton, and hung him to a tree near Hamilton & Hazlett's place at Old Agency. He exhibited no emotion, but appeared entirely indifferent in regard to his approaching end, and only requested the avenging party to

be sure and break his neck. The above facts were sworn to by Mr. Hamilton at the coroner's inquest held over the body of Stewart and before Judge Tattan. Mr. Hamilton swore that he did not recognize any of the party, and would not be able to identify any of them, and the coroner's jury brought in a verdict that Stewart "came to his death by hanging; that said hanging was committed by persons to the jury unknown." And so closed the earthly career of the perpetrator of one of the most fiendish and deliberate murders that disgrace the history of our Territory, the particulars of which, as gathered from the deposition of witnesses, are as follows:

Stewart came to Morgan's ranch two days before the murder. He told Morgan something about horses, and he and Morgan went out that day looking for horses. The next day he stayed around the house, evidently preparing the robbery and murder. It is not known whether he slept up stairs with Morgan the night preceding the murder, or whether he slept in the stable where he stayed the first night. Morgan slept up stairs, the steps leading to his room being on the outside of the house, and Mrs. Armstrong occupied a room down stairs, in which also were Maggie Houseman, a little girl of 12, and Annie Keogh, aged 6. The murderer first shot Morgan, the report of the gun waking Mrs. Armstrong, who asked, "What is that!" Stewart, who by this time must have come down stairs, said it was a coyote among the turkeys. Mrs. Armstrong told Maggie to get up and look after the turkeys. When Maggie got outside she saw Stewart with a gun, and asked him not to kill her, to which he answered "oh, no." When she returned he stood at the door of Mrs. Armstrong's room, with a gun in his hand. He fired two shots, the bullets striking Mrs. Armstrong behind the right shoulder. Maggie ran away then, but came back to get Annie Keogh, and at that time Mrs. Armstrong was lying in the sitting room, dead, and the murderer was going through the trunks and boxes. The little girl went upstairs and saw Morgan lying in bed, his mouth open and his eyes partly open and apparently dead. She got afraid and took Annie and ran to the brush opposite the house. While they were in the brush they saw the house burning, and saw a mare near by, and Maggie went back to the house and got a saddle, which she put on the mare, and her and Annie rode toward H. L. Kennerly's and on the way met that gentleman and told him of the murder. This was the substance of Maggie Housman's testimony, which was corroborated by Annie Keogh.

From the description given by the little girl Mr. Kennerly recognized Stewart as the man, and he and Mr. Hamilton arrested Stewart. Stewart was standing in front of the store with about fifteen other men, and was immediately recognized and singled out from the others by Maggie, and was also identified by Annie. A pair of blankets then in the possession of Stewart, and which he had not had a few days before, were proved to have belonged to Mrs. Armstrong.

There is no doubt, from the corroborative evidence, that Stewart was the murderer, and though lynch law is to be deprecated, the community will hardly find fault with the swift retribution meted out to the fiend in human shape who could thus deliberately commit such an atrocious crime for motives of gain, and the prompt punishment will go far toward preventing a similar crime.

News From Old Agency,
Mr. H. Brinkman returned from the Old Agency on Tuesday with twenty-seven head of horses. He tells us that everything is prosperous in that section and that the residents are in unusually good spirits. Mr. Brinkman arrived at Old Agency in time to assist in the burial of Morgan and Mrs. Armstrong, the victims of the fiend Stewart. The sad work of interment was performed by A. B. Hamilton and Mr. Brinkman. The latter saw also the place where Stewart was strung up and the grave in which his remains lie, not very deep down either. When the lynching job was well finished each of the men engaged in the work took a piece of the rope as a relic and the various articles he had on his person were also distributed among the committee as reminders of the deed they had done.

The cow boys will finish the round up in about eight days. The losses are very light.

Mr. Hamilton has plenty of nice, ripe strawberries and on the 4th of August he proposes to give a grand festival or strawberry treat. The editor has been invited to assist in the work of demolishing the luscious berry, and he would certainly be pleased to do so if the long distance did not intervene.

John Smith, of the celebrated Cottage saloon, Miles City, is having manufactured for him in the east an elegant championship billiard cue, which he will give to the best player. This magnificent cue cost $75.

The Yellowstone Journal has the following: "O. H. Morgan and Mrs. Armstrong were murdered June 29th in their cabin at the mouth of the Muddy, on the Missouri, and the cabin was then burned with their bodies inside. Two little daughters of Mrs. Armstrong, the oldest twelve years of age, escaped from the cabin and hid in the bushes until the cabin murderer was gone.
